title: 3. Distribution, Supply Chain & Unit Economics
book_title: Chapter 3: How It Is Sold & Delivered — Distribution & Unit Economics
question: How does a product travel from a vendor's factory to a customer's shelf, how much of each rupee of sales does Creative Newtech keep after funding the credit it extends, and what really explains the cash-flow whiplash between FY26 and H1 FY27?

epigraph.quote: we don't feel that, that is going to be sustainable in the long run.
epigraph.author: Ajit Thakur, CFO, Creative Newtech, Q2 FY27 earnings call, 29 October 2026 (on the 45-day working-capital figure)

web_blocks.text: Creative Newtech does not run one business. It runs three roads from a factory to a customer, and each road has its own margin, its own cash cycle and a different owner of the risk. In FY26 (audited, consolidated) the company booked revenue from operations of ₹2,704.62 Cr. That was made up of ₹2,699.77 Cr of product sales and ₹4.84 Cr of export entitlements. The segment note, the earnings call and the investor decks use the ₹2,699.77 Cr figure. Of that, the Market Entry Specialist segment was ₹2,318.92 Cr (86%) and the Brand Business was ₹380.86 Cr (14%) [15]. Total income, which adds ₹12.89 Cr of other income, was ₹2,717.51 Cr. Yet the brand segment produced ₹126.29 Cr of the ₹213.58 Cr segment result, or 59% [15]. That mismatch, 14% of the sales carrying 59% of the gross earnings, is the single most important fact about how the company is sold and delivered. It means the volume engine and the profit engine are different machines, and the volume engine is the one that eats the cash.

web_blocks.title: The go-to-market anatomy: three roads, three risk owners

web_blocks.caption: Three roads from factory to customer (FY26 consolidated unless stated; margins from the audited segment note and management commentary)
rows: 26+ global and domestic brands such as Samsung monitors, Cooler Master, ViewSonic, Lexar, Corsair and Zion [15]
Imports or buys locally, stocks across 18 warehouses, sells to 10,000+ channel partners, large format retail and e-commerce [15]
Resellers, retailers, marketplaces and quick-commerce platforms
Audited segment result of 3.76% of segment revenue [15]; management put enterprise gross margin at 2.09% in FY25, down from 2.61% [21]
Vendor credit funds stock, customer credit funds sales; festive quarters load both
Enterprise and solutions desk (branded Creative Advantage for Enterprise)
OEMs and Make-in-India brands such as Matrix, Sparsh and Supermicro [15][18]
Back-to-back orders to system integrators, PSUs and government portals; GeM orders of ₹54.15 Cr in FY26 [15]
Lowest margin of the three; management calls it an opportunity business [21]
Designed to need no capital, but Make-in-India vendors want advances and customers want credit [16]
Contract manufacturers across 28+ Asian facilities; the Honeywell trademark licensed from Honeywell International [15]
Designs, sources, quality-checks, markets and sells through a Hong Kong subsidiary, Secure Connection Limited [15]
Distributors in 38 countries, Amazon, Noon, Blinkit and Zepto [15]
Audited segment result of 33.2% of segment revenue [15]; CFO cites brand gross profit of 40% to 42% in H1 FY27 [17]
Brand model uses capital for 90 to 120 days, plus heavy marketing outlay [17]
web_blocks.takeaway: The same warehouse and the same people serve all three roads. Only the third earns a fat margin on each rupee, and only the first two absorb most of the working capital. The investor is therefore underwriting a thin-margin logistics base that subsidises, and is subsidised by, a licence-driven brand business. [15][17]

web_blocks.text: The physical footprint is modest for a business of this size. The annual report counts 31+ branches across India and 18 pan-India warehouses with 125,000+ sq. ft. of space. It adds more than 2,000 CBM of capacity in international warehouses in Mainland China and Dubai. The company also reports a network of 10,000+ channel partners across 38+ countries [15]. The Bhiwandi mother warehouse is authorised as a private bonded warehouse under the Customs Act. The company also holds AEO-T2 status. In plain terms, imported goods can then sit under customs control before duty is paid, and they clear faster [15]. FY26 volumes were 533 containers of imports and 55,453 domestic transactions [15]. The report counts 355 employees across the group, of whom 202 are permanent staff on the parent's own rolls [15]. Consolidated employee cost of ₹21.30 Cr is only 0.79% of revenue, so each group employee carries about ₹7.6 Cr of sales. That is lean, which is why operating leverage is real, but it also means the sales force is small relative to the 10,000 partners it serves.

Vendor terms are the quiet risk in this map. The IPO prospectus warned that distribution agreements may be renewed only at the partner's discretion. Partners can terminate by written notice, some with immediate effect. Some agreements are also non-exclusive, so a vendor may appoint other distributors in the same territory [19]. It also disclosed that the top ten suppliers were 52.79% of purchases and the top five 47.05% in FY2016 [19]. The FY26 annual report gives no current concentration figure. It says only that many partner brands have appointed Creative as exclusive partner and kept the association for over five years [15]. The other end of the chain is thinner still. Creative's own e-commerce arm, Creative eCommerce Ventures, is a 49% associate after two outside investors bought in during FY25. It contributed a ₹0.05 Cr share of loss in FY26 [15]. The marketplace road is therefore run mainly by selling to Amazon, Noon, Blinkit and peers, not through an owned storefront.

On the sourcing side the standalone company recorded imports of ₹455.84 Cr and export earnings of ₹754.03 Cr in FY26 [15]. Imports are paid partly through bank buyer's credit and partly out of cash credit lines. Those lines are payable on demand and carry 9% to 11% interest. They are secured on stock, book debts and property, with personal guarantees from the promoter directors [15]. The annual report says foreign-exchange risk is managed 'to the extent considered necessary' without giving a hedge ratio [15]. For a distributor whose Honeywell flows are largely dollar-priced, that is a disclosure gap rather than a proven problem. The consolidated translation reserve rose ₹8.62 Cr in FY26, a sign that currency moved in the company's favour in the year [15].

web_blocks.title: Real-World Walkthrough 1: One Honeywell air purifier, from a contract factory to a quick-commerce dark store
paragraphs: Customer and problem. A flat-owner in Delhi searches for an air purifier in November, when pollution peaks and Diwali firecrackers add to it. She wants a known brand, delivery in minutes and a price below the premium imports. Creative's answer is a Honeywell-branded purifier sold on Blinkit, Zepto, Swiggy Instamart or Amazon, where the company now has direct listings [15]. Management says Q3 is always the highest Honeywell quarter for exactly this reason: ₹98.23 Cr in Q3 FY25 against ₹65.40 Cr in Q4 [21].

What is built and by whom. Creative owns no factory for this. Honeywell licenses the trademark. Secure Connection Limited in Hong Kong, 77.5% owned by Creative, designs the product and picks a contract manufacturer from a pool of 28+ Asian facilities. It runs quality control from an office in China [15]. Honeywell first audits the factory, then approves every pack and product against its design language. It scores the licensee each quarter on a 1-to-5 scale. Creative reported its best-ever score of 4.8 on the 16 May 2025 call [21].

How it is priced, shipped, billed and collected. Goods move by sea to India, the Middle East and Southeast Asia. In the Middle East partners hold 45 to 60 days of stock. A Red Sea freight spike from $1,500-$1,700 to $7,500-$8,000 therefore hits the next restock, not the shelf today [16]. In India the company sells to dealers and platforms. For its new WOZOYO brand it refuses consignment or sale-or-return terms even if it loses sales, an unusual stance that Honeywell's pull makes affordable [17]. The royalty expense line in the audited notes is ₹5.96 Cr, 1.6% of Honeywell sales. We take it to be the Honeywell licence charge, although the note does not name the payee. Alongside it runs a stream of marketing spend that management put near ₹32 Cr to ₹33 Cr for the brand [15][16].

What it means for the business. Every purifier carries a gross margin several times that of a monitor or a memory card, yet the licence is borrowed, not owned. The consumer sees Honeywell, not Creative. If the licence moves, the factory network, the 38-country distributor list and the platform listings stay, but the brand premium goes with Honeywell. Chapter 4 prices that dependence in probability terms.

web_blocks.text: How Make-in-India sourcing and local assembly fit in matters for margin and for cash. In FY26 management began favouring Indian makers of surveillance, AI and components. As Ketan Patel put it on the 15 May 2026 call, these vendors are much smaller, so the distributor earns a higher percentage margin. But the same smallness means the vendors and their smaller customers cannot fund large orders, so Creative carries the credit [16]. The investor presentation concedes the trade-off: vendor credit remains limited, advances are higher and margins temporarily lower [18]. Other current assets rose from ₹113.98 Cr at March 2025 to ₹160.77 Cr at March 2026 and to ₹272.44 Cr by September 2026 [15][20]. Local assembly arrives through partners such as Infinova, whose small factory and assembly line sits inside the pending acquisition. Management says its camera sales fell from ₹38 Cr to ₹32 Cr last March for lack of STQC certification. It also says Creative needs ₹75 Cr in a full year to prove the thesis [17].

web_blocks.title: Pricing and gross-margin structure by segment

web_blocks.caption: Audited consolidated segment note, FY26 versus FY25 (₹ Cr; segment result is revenue after allocable cost and before finance cost and unallocated overheads)
web_blocks.takeaway: Brand revenue grew 41% and its result grew 35%. Market Entry revenue grew 54% and its result 59%, but Market Entry segment assets grew 2.7 times to ₹579.40 Cr. Growth in the low-margin road is being bought with balance sheet. [15]

web_blocks.text: Read the table as a gross-profit map. The company defines no gross margin line, but segment result is close to revenue less cost of goods and direct cost. The figures reconcile. The segment total of ₹213.58 Cr plus ₹4.84 Cr of export entitlements equals the ₹218.43 Cr difference between revenue from operations of ₹2,704.62 Cr and cost of goods of ₹2,486.19 Cr [15]. On that basis the blended FY26 gross margin is 8.08% of revenue from operations, against 8.80% in FY25. On total income, the basis the earnings decks use, it is 8.51%. It fell in the very year the low-margin road grew fastest [15]. Management gave a cleaner split on earlier calls. It cited channel gross margin of 6% to 7% and enterprise 2% to 2.5% [21]. It also cited a distribution blend near 3.9% for H1 FY26 [21] and brand gross profit of 40% to 42% in H1 FY27 [17]. The audited 33.2% brand figure is lower than the CFO's 40% to 42%. The filings do not reconcile the two definitions, so we use the audited figure for decisions.

The H1 FY27 results show what mix does. Consolidated gross margin rose to 11.34% in Q2 FY27 from 7.90% a year earlier. Mix drove the change, as the brand share of segment revenue moved from 14.1% in FY26 to 17.4% in H1 FY27 and 19.0% in Q2 FY27 [18][17]. The CFO attributed about 200 bps of the lift to the market-entry business itself and 350 bps in total [17]. Management's own gate for a new brand is 37% to 40% gross margin [17]. It is willing to forgo even a 22% margin only when the product needs no working capital. A distributor that sets such a gate is telling you that its channel margin cannot pay for the capital the channel consumes.

web_blocks.title: Credit terms, receivable days and who funds whom

web_blocks.caption: Working-capital ladder from audited and reviewed balance sheets (₹ Cr; days computed by us on the stated basis)
rows: Receivable days (on annual revenue; Sep-26 on Q2 FY27 revenue annualised)
Payable days (on cost of goods; Sep-26 is 66 on purchases)
web_blocks.takeaway: Receivables did not fall in H1 FY27; payables more than doubled. Borrowings dropped by ₹130.26 Cr because suppliers, not customers, financed the business. [15][20]

web_blocks.text: Credit quality looks clean even as the book grows. Of ₹565.11 Cr of receivables, 96.7% was less than six months past due and only ₹2.37 Cr was disputed. Related-party balances were ₹32.45 Cr (5.7%). The loss allowance is ₹0.77 Cr, or 0.14% of the book, after a fresh ₹0.54 Cr charge in FY26 [15]. Receivable days still moved from 49 to 76, which the receivables turnover ratio confirms: 6.73 times against 9.22 times a year earlier [15]. Ketan Patel told the call that average receivables run at 48 to 50 days and should fall back to a 13% to 14% share of turnover [16]. Our computation on the audited balance is 76 days. The two numbers coexist because the March balance carries a quarter that grew 84% year on year, from ₹402.99 Cr to ₹740.01 Cr [18]. A year-end snapshot of a seasonal, back-loaded business overstates the average, but an average of 48 to 50 days has not been demonstrated by the filings.

Financing is conventional rather than exotic. The filings disclose no factoring or bill-discounting programme. Funding is cash credit repayable on demand at 9% to 11%, buyer's credit for imports, and a supplier-finance line on the government's TReDS platform. That line carried about ₹171 Cr at March 2026 and equalled 53% of total borrowings of ₹324.26 Cr [15][16]. Management explains that MSME vendors must be paid within 45 days, and that this borrowing costs 8% to 9% [16]. The annual report's own ratios show debt to equity moving from 0.24 to 0.89 and interest cover from 9.96 times to 6.09 times in FY26, on the report's own definitions. The stricter EBIT-to-interest cover in Chapter 6 is about 5.0 times for FY26 [15]. Finance cost doubled to ₹20.66 Cr. H1 FY27 already carries ₹16.92 Cr, 82% of the FY26 total, because borrowings stayed high until the September-quarter payable stretch [15][20].

Seasonality drives all of this. Quarterly revenue from operations in FY26 ran ₹392.96 Cr, ₹655.01 Cr, ₹911.79 Cr and ₹740.01 Cr. Q3 alone was 34% of the year, and the October-to-March half was 61% [18]. Management calls the October-to-December quarter 'our most significant quarter' [21]. It explains that retailers now take delivery 20 to 25 days before a festival because their warehouses switch to outbound-only during it [17]. The Diwali date moved a month later in 2026. That shifts part of the festive stocking out of Q2 and into Q3, and may explain why Q2 total income grew only 14% [17][18]. For cash, the pattern is stocking, then selling, then collecting. Receivables swell at September and again at March, and the credit extended to a retailer in September is collected well into the winter.

web_blocks.title: What actually drove the FY26 outflow and the H1 FY27 inflow

web_blocks.caption: Consolidated operating cash flow bridge (₹ Cr; FY26 audited, H1 columns reviewed; positive adds cash)
rows: Other financial and current assets (mostly vendor advances)
web_blocks.takeaway: The FY26 hole was receivables. The H1 FY27 recovery was payables and other liabilities, which together added ₹474.73 Cr, while receivables, vendor advances and stock still absorbed ₹181.02 Cr. [15][20]

web_blocks.text: Management's account of FY26 is internally consistent and mostly confirmed. The CFO said receivables rose from ₹237.77 Cr to ₹565.11 Cr, from 13.4% to about 21% of turnover. He gave two reasons: the last quarter's sales nearly doubled, and the new AI, surveillance and data-centre lines require extended credit to settle in [16]. The audited statement agrees on size: receivables absorbed ₹327.34 Cr, which is 4.7 times the year's profit after tax of ₹70.29 Cr [15]. The audited FY26 cash flow from operations is a ₹271.88 Cr outflow. The Q2 FY27 presentation prints this as ₹271.88 Cr on one page and ₹273.10 Cr on another, and we use the audited ₹271.88 Cr [15][18]. One further effect is classification. The TReDS lines are shown as borrowings, so about ₹171 Cr of supplier payments sits in financing. On a view that treats TReDS as supplier credit, the FY26 outflow would be about ₹101 Cr [15][16].

The H1 FY27 story needs a harder look. The presentation says 'earnings growth was backed by strong cash conversion, reflecting the focus on tighter control over receivables, inventory and payables' [18]. The cash-flow statement says receivables rose ₹51.60 Cr, inventories rose ₹13.03 Cr and other assets rose ₹116.39 Cr in the half. Operating profit before working capital was only ₹63.11 Cr. The ₹351.24 Cr inflow came from trade payables up ₹281.90 Cr and other liabilities up ₹192.83 Cr [20]. Payables went from ₹185.11 Cr to ₹467.01 Cr, and the other-current-liabilities line from ₹19.08 Cr to ₹215.90 Cr [15][20]. At March that line was largely customer advances. The September split is not in the results filing, so we treat the jump as probable project advances rather than proven. The CFO himself said the vendor terms were negotiated 'very hard' but are 'not sustainable'. He guided to 52 to 55 net working-capital days rather than the reported 45 [17].

Our reading is that the H1 FY27 inflow is real cash but is of lower quality than the headline. Over eighteen months the company generated ₹79.35 Cr of operating cash flow (−₹271.88 Cr plus ₹351.24 Cr) against ₹109.76 Cr of profit after tax. That is 72% conversion, which is acceptable for a business that grew its revenue base by half. We think it is more likely than not, roughly a 70% chance, that a meaningful share of the payable and customer-advance build reverses over the next two to three quarters. The reasons are that vendor terms normalise and the Q3 festive stocking draws cash. The investor should treat a normalised cash conversion of 50% to 70% of profit as the planning range. The nearly nine times profit that the H1 FY27 inflow represents is not a planning basis.

web_blocks.caption: Where ₹100 of FY26 revenue goes, from billing to free cash flow (audited consolidated, ₹ Cr base)
web_blocks.takeaway: Of every ₹100 billed, ₹91.92 buys goods, ₹4.71 runs the company, ₹0.76 pays interest, ₹0.42 goes to tax and ₹2.60 is reported profit. Because receivables absorbed ₹12.10 per ₹100, free cash flow was a negative ₹10.17. [15]

web_blocks.text: Walk the ₹100 down slowly. Goods, net of the stock build, take ₹91.92. Employees take ₹0.79 and all other expenses ₹3.92, so earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and other income are ₹3.37, which matches the 3.4% operating margin in the filings. Depreciation takes ₹0.06, interest ₹0.76, and other income of ₹0.47 comes back, so pre-tax profit is ₹3.02. Tax, at an effective 14%, leaves ₹2.60 of reported profit [15]. The company's own EBITDA figure is ₹103.95 Cr, 3.84% of revenue from operations. On total income it is 3.83%, the margin the company prints. The figure includes the other income and the associate loss [15]. Now step to cash. Working capital took ₹13.38 per ₹100 of revenue and income tax paid ₹0.37. After the non-cash add-backs, the bridge row in the waterfall nets to −₹12.71, so operating cash flow was −₹10.05. After ₹0.12 of fixed-asset spend, free cash flow was −₹10.17 per ₹100 [15]. A business that keeps ₹2.60 of paper profit while consuming ₹10 of cash per ₹100 of sales is financed by someone else. In FY26 that someone was the banking system, which advanced ₹254.72 Cr net [15].

Now a single-unit worked example, built only from audited ratios. Suppose Creative buys goods for ₹100. At the FY26 blended mix it sells them for ₹108.79, a gross margin of ₹8.79. Staff and other expenses take ₹5.12, depreciation ₹0.06 and interest ₹0.83. Other income adds ₹0.52 and tax removes ₹0.46, so ₹2.83 is left [15]. The financing arithmetic explains why that is so thin. If Creative had to fund the ₹108.79 receivable for 76 days at 10% from bank debt alone, interest would be ₹2.27, or 26% of the gross margin. On the Market Entry segment's 3.76% margin, the same ₹100 sells for ₹103.91 and leaves ₹3.91 gross. After 76 days of carry less 27 days of supplier credit, the net financing cost is about ₹1.42, or 36% of the gross margin. On the Honeywell road, ₹100 sells for ₹149.61, leaves ₹49.61 and 105 days of carry costs ₹4.30, or 9%. Those are our illustrations using a 10% rate, not company disclosures, but they show why management keeps raising the share of the brand road.

web_blocks.title: Real-World Walkthrough 2: A government fibre order, from advance work order to cash
paragraphs: Customer and problem. Bharat Sanchar Nigam Limited needs a middle-mile fibre network for the Odisha telecom circle under BharatNet. Creative and a consortium partner received an advance work order with an approximate total value of ₹3,194.83 Cr. The order includes a capex phase and several years of operation and maintenance [17].

How it is priced and built. Management describes about ₹1,700 Cr of capex over roughly 3.5 years and about ₹1,200 Cr of operating revenue over the following seven years. Creative orders pipe, GIS survey work and network equipment. BSNL inspects vendor factories and the bill of materials. An independent engineer certifies progress on a digital tracker [17].

How it is billed and collected. Revenue is recognised only after BSNL quality certification. The CFO expects ₹100 Cr to ₹150 Cr in FY27 and about ₹500 Cr the year after. The chairman guided to ₹150 Cr to ₹200 Cr in Q4 FY27 and ₹500 Cr to ₹600 Cr in FY28, at a net margin of 6% to 7% of billing [17]. Cash goes out to vendors months before BSNL certifies and pays, so this order will test working capital harder than the festive cycle does.

What it means for the business. A ₹500 Cr annual billing line at 6% to 7% net would add ₹30 Cr to ₹35 Cr of profit, roughly half of FY26's total. But it arrives through the road that needs the most advances. The 45-day working-capital figure is the number to watch as this order ramps up.

web_blocks.text: The ultimate takeaway for Chapter 3 is that the distribution model is sound in its mechanics and fragile in its funding. The mechanics are a lean, bonded, 18-warehouse network and a 10,000-partner channel. They also include direct listings on the fastest-growing retail formats and a brand road that converts a borrowed trademark into a 33% segment margin. The fragility is a low-margin road that tripled its asset base in a year. The cash-flow recovery came from suppliers and advances. Management also still has to prove it can bring the year-end receivable ratio back to the 13% to 14% it targets [15][16][20]. We rate the chance that FY27 closes with operating cash flow above reported profit as roughly even, because the September payable level must hold through the stocking quarter.

book_paragraphs: Stand with me for a moment at the dispatch bay of a Bhiwandi warehouse on a September evening. A container of monitors has arrived from a factory in Asia, another is being unloaded with Honeywell air purifiers, and a third lorry is leaving for a Chandigarh retailer who wants his Diwali stock in his shop twenty-five days before the festival starts. Creative Newtech's whole business is this choreography. In FY26 it moved 533 containers of imports and executed 55,453 domestic transactions, through 18 warehouses and 31-plus branches, with just 355 people across the group and 202 on the parent's permanent rolls. Do you see what that implies? Employee cost is under one rupee per hundred of sales. The company is a very thin layer between a vendor's factory and a customer's shelf, and everything we care about, margin, risk and cash, comes from how thick or thin that layer is on each road.

There are three roads, and I want you to learn them by heart. The first is channel distribution: Samsung monitors, Cooler Master cases, Lexar cards. Creative buys, stores and sells to ten thousand partners, and earns, on the audited segment note, about 3.8 paise for every rupee. The second is the enterprise desk, which management itself describes as a back-to-back business where, as Ketan Patel put it on the 18 August 2023 call, 'we don't invest any money'. The third is the Honeywell and owned-brand road, where Creative designs, specifies, markets and sells goods built by contract factories, and earns 33 paise per rupee on the same note. Eighty-six percent of sales travel the first two roads. Fifty-nine percent of the gross earnings come from the third. Hold that asymmetry in your head; it recurs in every chapter.

Before we price an invoice, ask who can walk away. Creative's partner brands are not captives. The 2017 prospectus warned that vendors may renew 'at the discretion of partners', may terminate on written notice and may appoint other distributors where an agreement is non-exclusive. In FY2016 its top ten suppliers were 52.79 percent of purchases. The FY26 annual report is gentler, noting that many brands have named Creative their exclusive partner and stayed for more than five years, but it gives no current concentration number. I read that silence carefully. It is not proof of a problem; it is a gap in what the shareholder can verify, and distribution is a business where a single lost order can erase a quarter's growth, as Ketan Patel reminded the 16 May 2025 call when he said that in the first quarter of FY25 the company 'lost a sale of almost INR200 crore plus' in enterprise.

Let me walk you through an invoice on the first road. A reseller in Jaipur orders thirty monitors. Creative's purchase cost might be ₹100 per unit of value; it sells at about ₹103.91, so the gross margin is ₹3.91. That is before warehouse charges, salaries and interest. Then the credit sits there. The audited ratios put receivable days at 76 and payable days at 27, so Creative lends the reseller money for forty-nine days longer than its supplier lends to Creative. At a 10 percent cost of money, those forty-nine days of net carry cost about ₹1.42 per hundred, which is more than a third of the gross margin. This is why the distribution trade lives on volume and discipline, and why Ketan Patel said on the 17 May 2024 call that if enterprise orders do not earn a 20 percent return on capital, 'then we will not do that business because capital is limited'.

Now the second road, where the Make-in-India shift has changed the rules. Until two years ago, Creative's vendors were mostly multinationals who gave long credit and shipped from big plants. Surveillance and AI brought in smaller Indian makers who cannot finance a big order, so Creative pays them in advance, and whose customers, often government departments, pay late. Ketan Patel explained the margin side on the 15 May 2026 call: the vendors' 'size is much smaller and that's why you get a higher percentage margin'. The CFO explained the cash side: 'to get into the new area, we have to extend the extended credit'. Both statements are true and both appear in the numbers. Gross margin rose and vendor advances rose; other current assets went from ₹114 Cr to ₹161 Cr over FY26 and to ₹272 Cr by September 2026.

Then there is Honeywell, and I want you to picture what it is not. It is not a factory. Secure Connection Limited in Hong Kong, 77.5 percent owned by Creative, holds the trademark licence and runs a fabless model across 28-plus contract facilities in Asia, with its own quality-control office in China and outsourced logistics. It sells to distributors in 38 countries and to Amazon, Noon, Shopee, Lazada, Blinkit and Zepto. Its royalty expense line, which I take to be the Honeywell licence charge, is just ₹5.96 Cr, about 1.6 percent of Honeywell sales, and the royalty barely moved when Brand revenue rose 41 percent. Mentor-to-student: when you see a cost line that does not scale with revenue, ask who set it and when it resets. The answer here is a licence that renews in five-year blocks and that Ketan Patel said on the 15 May 2026 call 'will come for renewal in March 2027'.

The brand road has one more mechanic that investors miss: it borrows from the distribution road. Ketan Patel was blunt about it on the same call: while building Honeywell it 'was very dependent on the market entry business because the cash flows, the infrastructure, everything was used of this business'. The Honeywell team uses the same warehouses, the same finance team and the same bank lines. That is why a segment with ₹122 Cr of assets can earn ₹126 Cr of segment result, and also why the 33 percent number flatters it: the brand pays no rent for the shared infrastructure, and the low-margin road pays it. Management's plan is to separate the two businesses in two to three years, but not for the next fifteen months. Until then you should read the segment note as a gross-profit map, not a stand-alone profit and loss.

Look now at how the calendar shapes the cash. FY26 revenue by quarter was ₹393 Cr, ₹655 Cr, ₹912 Cr and ₹740 Cr. Q3 alone was 34 percent of the year, and the October-to-March half was 61 percent. Ketan Patel told the 29 October 2026 call why: retailers now take delivery 'at least 20, 25 days before the festival starts', and during the festival their warehouses are 'only outbound'. So the sale happens in September and the cash comes in November. Add a Diwali that fell a month later this year and you can see why Q2 FY27 total income grew only 14 percent while the biggest quarter still lies ahead. A year-end balance sheet in March therefore holds the debt and the receivables of a busy season, which is probably why a March snapshot of 76 receivable days looks so much worse than the 48 to 50 that management quotes as the average.

Now to the question that made me pick up this file: why did operating cash flow swing from a ₹271.88 Cr outflow in FY26 to a ₹351.24 Cr inflow in H1 FY27? In FY26 the answer is in plain sight. Receivables rose ₹327.34 Cr, 4.7 times the year's profit, because Q4 revenue jumped 84 percent and because the new lines need credit. Ajit Thakur said receivables would normalise; Ketan Patel said they 'should fall back to the original number'. There is a second effect. About ₹171 Cr of supplier payments were routed through TReDS borrowings, so a part of the outflow is a classification effect: treat TReDS as supplier credit and the FY26 outflow shrinks to about ₹101 Cr. Both effects are legitimate, and I want you to hold both in mind when someone quotes you the headline.

The H1 FY27 reversal is where I stop nodding along. The presentation says it came from 'tighter control over receivables, inventory and payables'. I read the cash-flow statement line by line, and it says otherwise. Receivables rose ₹51.60 Cr. Inventories rose ₹13.03 Cr. Vendor advances in other assets rose ₹116.39 Cr. What produced the inflow was trade payables, up ₹281.90 Cr, from ₹185.11 Cr to ₹467.01 Cr, and other liabilities, up ₹192.83 Cr. The CFO was honest about it on the 29 October call: 'we don't feel that, that is going to be sustainable in the long run', and he guided to 52 to 55 days. So ask yourself what you would do with a half-year of cash that is rented from suppliers: spend it on growth, or hold it against the day they ask for it back?

Let me give you the arithmetic that keeps me balanced about this. Across the eighteen months the company generated ₹79.35 Cr of operating cash on ₹109.76 Cr of profit, a 72 percent conversion. That is not a failure; for a business that grew its revenue base by half it is respectable. But the composition changed. In FY26 the debt was the shock absorber: borrowings rose from ₹71.80 Cr to ₹324.26 Cr. In H1 FY27 suppliers took that role: borrowings fell to ₹194.00 Cr and cash rose to ₹206.36 Cr. Neither funding source is free, and neither is permanent. My own estimate, and I hold it at roughly 70 percent, is that a sizeable part of the payable stretch reverses within two or three quarters, particularly through the Q3 stocking cycle.

Here is the same story as pennies. Out of every ₹100 Creative billed in FY26, ₹91.92 bought goods after stock changes, ₹0.79 paid staff, ₹3.92 paid everything else, ₹0.06 was depreciation, ₹0.76 was interest, ₹0.42 went to tax, and ₹2.60 was reported profit. Receivables absorbed ₹12.10 of the ₹100, stock ₹2.44 and other assets ₹1.54, while payables added back ₹2.71, so operating cash flow was −₹10.05 and, after ₹0.12 of capital spending, free cash flow was −₹10.17. Think about what that says. Creative reported profit and paid taxes on it, while the bank funded the sales. That is normal for a distributor in a growth year, and it is the reason a 2.6 percent margin demands a credit officer's discipline more than a marketer's imagination.

What should a careful investor take from this chapter? First, the mechanics are sensible. The footprint is lean, the bonded warehouse and customs status are useful, the platform listings are well chosen, and credit losses are tiny. Second, the profit engine is the brand road and the cash engine is the channel road, and they share a balance sheet. Third, the FY26 outflow was a real, receivables-led build, partly reclassified by TReDS; and the H1 FY27 recovery was mostly supplier and advance money that management itself calls temporary. Fourth, management's willingness to say so aloud is a point in its favour. I would watch the receivable ratio and the payable days each quarter. If payable days drift back toward 30 without receivable days falling, the next cash-flow headline will be a repeat of FY26.

book_callouts.title: NARRATOR'S REFLECTION
book_callouts.text: I have read many distributors' cash-flow statements and the pattern is almost always the same: a growth year burns cash, a stretch year borrows it back from suppliers, and the honest question is which of the two the next year will resemble. What I value in this file is that the CFO named the stretch as unsustainable before anyone had to ask. What I do not yet know is whether the 52 to 55 day target is a real operating plan or a comfortable range. I would feel better if the receivable ratio, and not the payables line, did the work in the next set of numbers.

book_callouts.title: MENTAL MODEL: THE CREDIT SANDWICH
book_callouts.text: A distributor is a sandwich: vendor credit above, customer credit below, thin margin in the middle. Profit shows up in the filling; cash is decided by the bread. Check three numbers every quarter, receivable days, payable days and the gap between them, and you will see cash trouble a quarter before the income statement does.
